title: In the Weeds: The Importance of Knowledge
author: benzulauf
summary: The benzulauf newsletter synthesizes Paul Kirschner's concept of 'useless knowledge' and Carl Hendrick's idea of 'learning at the edge of understanding' to make a case for broad, seemingly impractical knowledge as both intrinsically valuable and strategically essential for effective storytelling, teaching, and thinking. Kirschner's point (originally intended as an endorsement) is that knowledge which appears useless from a narrow utility perspective is exactly the knowledge that produces the most unexpected connections, the richest analogies, and the most creative insights -- because by definition, high-utility knowledge is what everyone has, while 'useless' knowledge is what creates distinctiveness. Hendrick's complementary point is that learning at the edge of understanding -- engaging with material that is slightly beyond current mastery -- requires a broad base of already-mastered knowledge from which to reach. The piece applies these insights to teaching and writing: the teacher and writer with the broadest knowledge base generates the most illuminating analogies, the most unexpected connections, and the most memorable examples.
points: * Kirschner's 'useless knowledge' insight inverts the common critique: knowledge that appears useless from a narrow utility perspective is exactly the knowledge that produces unexpected connections and creative insights, because everyone already has high-utility knowledge. * Hendrick's 'edge of understanding' concept is interdependent with broad knowledge: learning at the edge requires a wide base to reach from -- the student with a narrow knowledge base has a narrow edge and limited capacity for productive cognitive stretch. * For teachers and writers, broad knowledge is a professional asset: it generates illuminating analogies, unexpected connections, and memorable examples that narrow expertise cannot produce. * The piece makes a positive case for 'knowing things for their own sake' as the most reliable path to useful creativity: the person who reads widely across domains will find connections that the domain expert misses. * The synthesis of Kirschner and Hendrick produces a strong argument for knowledge-rich curriculum: broad knowledge makes students better learners (by widening their edge), better thinkers (by enabling unexpected connections), and better communicators (by expanding their analogy bank).
quotes: Kirschner calls it useless knowledge. He means it as a compliment. The knowledge that appears most useless -- the fact about an obscure historical period, the biological detail that has no obvious application, the philosophical argument that no one will pay you for -- that is exactly the knowledge that produces the connection no one else makes, because no one else has it.

Hendrick's idea of learning at the edge is beautiful and demanding. You learn best at the edge of what you already know. But the width of your edge depends entirely on the breadth of your prior knowledge. A narrow expert has a narrow edge and can only stretch in one direction. A broad learner has a wide edge and can stretch in any direction.

The teacher with the broadest knowledge base gives the best explanations. Not because breadth is inherently virtuous, but because explanation requires analogy, and analogy requires having something in your head that is structurally similar to the thing you're trying to explain. The broader the knowledge base, the more analogy options you have.

I read things that have nothing to do with what I teach. I read about medieval grain storage and twentieth-century jazz theory and the physiology of sleep. None of it is directly useful. All of it has turned up unexpectedly in lessons, in conversations, in moments when I needed a connection I hadn't planned for.

The case for knowledge-rich curriculum is not just about what students will know. It is about what kind of thinkers they will become. A student who has been taught a lot about the world has more to think with. The quality of thinking is bounded by the quantity and quality of the raw material available to it.
